title: QuoteFlow: voice-to-estimate for contractors (HF26 Side Hustle)
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

QuoteFlow turns messy jobsite notes (voice or text) into an itemized, region-aware estimate a contractor can send the same evening — materials, labor, equipment, permits, tax, branded PDF, and a copy/SMS/WhatsApp send loop.

Who would pay: solo plumbers, electricians, HVAC techs, and remodelers. They lose jobs when the quote lands late, and they lose evenings writing spreadsheets. Their alternatives are expensive quoting SaaS that wants the whole client list in someone else’s cloud, or a notes app plus hand math. QuoteFlow is the wrench-priced tool: fast bids, professional PDFs, and client addresses that do not need to be pasted into a generic cloud chatbot.

On the Windows desktop / Tauri path, open-weight Gemma runs via Ollama so job notes can stay on the PC. On the hosted demo (weak laptops / judges), Groq serves the same open-weight Gemma family with customer PII redacted before the cloud call.

Demo

Live app quoteflow-frontend-qlqc.onrender.com
API health quoteflow-backend-q60x.onrender.com/api/health
Repo github.com/Mavros-Lykos/QuoteFlow
Walkthrough YouTube

Try it in ~2 minutes: open the live demo → Try it in your browser → finish Welcome (pick India / INR / GST if you like) → New estimate → describe a plumbing job → Create → Send / PDF.

Screenshots

Landing

First-run setup (region-aware)

Voice-first new estimate

Generated estimate + send

Code

Repo: https://github.com/Mavros-Lykos/QuoteFlow

Stack in short:

  • Frontend: React + Vite PWA (optional Tauri desktop shell)
  • Backend: FastAPI + SQLite (Tiger Data / pgvector when the connection string connects)
  • Models: Gemma via Ollama on desktop; Groq Gemma on Render
  • Pricing path: TabPFN-style calibration on suggested totals; SerpApi labor grounding when keyed
  • Voice: ElevenLabs STT/TTS when keyed; browser speech fallback

How I Built It

  1. Welcome captures business + region (currency, tax name, units) so the UI, LLM prompts, and PDF stay consistent — e.g. INR + GST 18%.
  2. Job notes (mic or text) go to the open-weight model, which drafts an itemized BOM and a customer-facing proposal.
  3. Deterministic layers own money: line math, tax, TabPFN-style win-rate calibration on the suggested total.
  4. Optional partners enrich without owning the core path: SerpApi for live labor benchmarks, ElevenLabs for voice, Tiger Data hybrid memory (SQLite always; pgvector when TIGER_DATA_CONNECTION_STRING connects).
  5. Render hosts the judge-facing demo so nobody has to install Ollama to try it.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Privacy is the product for trades. Client names, addresses, and what’s broken inside someone’s home should not be the default paste into a closed chatbot. Local Gemma on desktop keeps that data on the machine after setup; the hosted path redacts PII before Groq.
  • Unit economics for a side-hustle tool. A one-person plumbing business will not justify $40/month SaaS for evening quotes. Open weights (local, or cheap hosted open models) keep marginal AI cost low enough that the product can be priced like a tool.
  • No lock-in at the worst moment. The estimating path is not tied to one proprietary model. Swap Ollama models on desktop; keep shipping when a vendor changes pricing.

Prize Categories

Each category below is a job QuoteFlow actually does on the live demo or desktop path — not a logo dump.

  • Best Use of Gemma — Gemma is the estimator, not a chatbot bolted on the side. Job notes become an itemized BOM and a customer-ready proposal; on desktop that is Ollama + open-weight Gemma on the contractor’s machine, and on the hosted demo the same open-weight family runs via Groq so judges can try it without a GPU. The privacy and “wrench-priced tool” story only works because the core model is open-weight.
  • Best Use of Render — Render is the shop floor for this Side Hustle: a public PWA frontend and FastAPI backend so a plumber (or a judge) can finish Welcome → estimate → PDF in a browser. The product is meant to be used at the end of a workday — if it only runs on my laptop, it is a prototype; Render makes it a real try-before-you-buy demo.
  • Best Use of TabPFN — Quoting is a tabular decision: win rate vs. margin. After Gemma drafts line items, a TabPFN-style calibration pass nudges the suggested total toward a price that can actually win the job — prediction inside the estimating agent, not a disconnected CSV notebook.
  • Best Use of SerpApi — Labor rates drift by ZIP and trade. When keyed, SerpApi grounds those rates in live market search so the estimate is not pure model guesswork; when offline, a regional index keeps the path honest. Fresh web signal feeding the quote, not a generic search widget.
  • Best Use of ElevenLabs — Hands are dirty, the phone is in a pocket. ElevenLabs STT/TTS turns “describe the job” into a voice-first loop (with browser speech as fallback), so the contractor can dictate once and send — exactly how a side hustle tool should feel after a long day on site.
  • Best Use of Tiger Data — Job memory is hybrid by design: SQLite always works; Tiger Cloud + pgvector kicks in when TIGER_DATA_CONNECTION_STRING connects, so similar past jobs can inform the next estimate without forcing every quote into a brittle single store. Embeddings and hybrid recall for the agent that remembers the last remodel, not just the last prompt.
  • Best Use of Mastra — The optional Mastra sidecar under mastra/ is the orchestration lane for multi-step estimate flows (tools + memory) when you want an agent harness around the same open models — same product, clearer separation between “UI app” and “agent workflow.”

Bonus — first user energy

I dogfooded the full path on the live Render demo (Welcome → plumbing job → estimate QF-20261019-style → Send sheet / PDF). The product pitch to a real plumber is the same as the demo: finish the physical workday, dictate the job once, send a branded estimate before dinner.

title: QuoteCraft: an offline AI that turns messy client WhatsApps into instant quotations and scopes
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

If you do any freelance work, consulting, or run a small service business, you know this exact message. It arrives on WhatsApp or Instagram DM at 10 PM:

"hi vikram! need a landing page for our boutique bakery in dehradun with menu, photo gallery, online order enquiry form connected to whatsapp, and google maps location. we have logo and photos ready. how much will this cost and can we get it before diwali? also need 3 revisions and basic seo."

Clients don't send neat requirement specifications. They send messy, conversational thoughts.

And that puts freelancers in a bad dilemma:

  1. If you delay responding, you lose the client to someone faster.
  2. If you send a quick casual price ("maybe ₹20,000"), you get trapped in endless scope creep — the client later asks for payment gateway integrations, copywriting, and 12 revision rounds that you never agreed to do for free.
  3. If you sit down to write a proper quote, it takes 45 minutes of manual typing to draft deliverables, milestones, payment terms, and boundaries.

Quoting tools like PandaDoc or HoneyBook charge $19 to $49 every single month. For a solo freelancer starting out, that is a huge recurring bill. Worse, pasting confidential client ideas, client phone numbers, and private business budgets into third-party cloud AI APIs can violate client NDAs and privacy.

So I built QuoteCraft: a small, fast local web app that turns messy client WhatsApp messages into an itemized quotation, a scope-of-work, and a ready-to-send WhatsApp reply in about 15 seconds.

It runs 100% on a laptop using a local open-weight model (Llama 3.2 via Ollama). Zero cloud APIs, zero per-token cost, and confidential client details never leave your machine.

Demo

Here is how QuoteCraft handles that real WhatsApp message for a boutique bakery in Dehradun:

1. The Itemized Scope of Work

QuoteCraft parses the message and builds a clean deliverables table with realistic timelines and pricing:

Deliverable Estimated Days Estimated Cost (INR)
UI/UX Design & Responsive Layout — Mobile-first modern design matching bakery aesthetic 3 Days ₹ 7,500
Digital Menu & Photo Gallery — Filterable categories with high-res photo showcase 2 Days ₹ 5,000
WhatsApp Order Integration & Maps — Direct one-tap ordering & Google Maps embed 2 Days ₹ 4,500
On-Page SEO & Speed Optimization — Local search optimization & 90+ Lighthouse speed 1 Day ₹ 3,000
Total Estimated Investment 8 Days ₹ 20,000

Every row is interactive and editable. If you want to change a price, adjust days, or add a custom task, you can edit it right in the table, and the total recalculates automatically.

2. The Anti-Scope Creep Shield (What is OUT of Scope)

This is what freelancers usually forget to write, and what costs them money later. QuoteCraft automatically specifies what is not included:

  • ⚠️ Paid domain registration and annual web hosting charges (paid directly by client)
  • ⚠️ Food photography and copywriting for menu item descriptions (provided by client)
  • ⚠️ Payment gateway merchant account registration (direct WhatsApp orders are included)
  • ⚠️ Revisions exceeding 3 review rounds (billed separately at standard hourly rate)

3. One-Click WhatsApp Reply

Freelancers don't want to copy a rigid 5-page PDF into a chat. QuoteCraft generates a polite, friendly WhatsApp message pre-formatted with bold tags (*text*) and emojis:

Hi Anita! 🧁 Thanks so much for reaching out.

I'd love to build the landing page for your bakery in Dehradun! Here is a quick quotation and timeline:

*Scope:*
• Custom mobile-friendly design with your logo & photos
• Interactive menu & photo gallery
• Direct WhatsApp ordering button (customers tap to order)
• Google Maps location & local SEO
• 3 review rounds included

*Timeline:* 8-10 business days (well before Diwali! 🪔)
*Total Investment:* ₹20,000 (40% advance to start)

Does this work for you? If yes, I can share the invoice and get started this Wednesday! 🙌

You hit "Copy WhatsApp Reply", paste it into your chat, and you are done in 30 seconds.

4. Print / Save as PDF

For formal corporate clients who need a paper trail, hitting Print renders an elegant, print-ready quotation sheet with quote reference ID, date, your business header, payment terms, and signature line.

Code

VIKRAM-009 / quotecraft

💼 QuoteCraft

Turn messy client WhatsApp messages into professional quotations, scope-of-work, and ready-to-send replies in seconds.

A local, privacy-first AI tool built for freelancers, solo agencies, and small service businesses.

🤔 The Problem

Every freelancer, solo developer, designer, photographer, and local business owner knows this pain:

A client sends a rambling, messy message on WhatsApp or Instagram at 10 PM:

"hey bro need website for my bakery in dehradun with online menu, photo gallery, online order enquiry form connected to whatsapp, and google maps location. we have logo ready. how much will this cost and can we get it before diwali? also need 3 revisions and basic seo."

Responding takes 30 to 60 minutes of tedious work:

  1. Translating messy thoughts into clear deliverables
  2. Estimating realistic days and pricing
  3. Setting milestones and advance deposit terms
  4. Setting boundaries against scope creep (so you don't end up doing unpaid extra work!)

Because writing…

View on GitHub

The entire app is one Python file (app.py), using only Flask and Python's standard library (urllib, json, re). It requires zero API keys and zero external services.

How I Built It

The stack:

Part What I used
Brain / Extraction & Pricing Llama 3.2 (3B) running locally via Ollama
Web Application Python 3.10 + Flask (single file, lightweight)
Structured Output Strict JSON schema enforced by Ollama's format parameter
UI & Offline Export Clean vanilla HTML5, CSS3 responsive grid, print stylesheet
Local Storage Local quotes.json file for private history log

I built and tested all of it on a normal laptop: Ubuntu, 15 GB RAM, and no GPU.

1. Enforcing Strict JSON Schemas

Smaller open models can sometimes add conversational chatter ("Sure, here is your quotation:") or hallucinate keys. To make the UI 100% reliable, I used Ollama's structured output format:

payload = {
    "model": "llama3.2",
    "messages": [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message}
    ],
    "format": QUOTE_SCHEMA,  # Enforces exact JSON keys
    "options": {"temperature": 0.2}
}

Setting temperature: 0.2 keeps the pricing estimates and deliverable breakdown consistent and grounded.

2. Protecting Against Scope Creep by Design

In the system prompt, I made "Out of Scope" a mandatory output field. If the client asked for a website, Llama 3.2 proactively flags domain hosting, photo shoots, and extra revisions as out of scope. That single design decision transforms the app from a generic text generator into a real business tool.

3. Problems I Hit (and What I Learned):

  • Ollama CPU cold starts: When Llama 3.2 first loads from disk into RAM on a CPU laptop, it took ~35 seconds. I set timeout=300 on the HTTP request so it never aborts prematurely during the first load. Once in memory, subsequent queries run much faster (~15-20s).
  • Markdown fence leaks: Even with format: json, some model variations wrap output in ```json ... ``` . I added a small regex cleaner to strip markdown code blocks before calling json.loads().
  • Zero-cost, responsive UI: Instead of loading heavy CSS frameworks from external CDNs (which fail when you have no internet), I wrote a clean vanilla CSS stylesheet with a responsive grid and a custom @media print style. The entire app loads instantly even with airplane mode turned on.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For QuoteCraft, open-source AI is not just a nice feature — it is the only reason this tool makes commercial sense:

  1. Client Confidentiality & Privacy (No NDA Breaches):
    When freelancers quote for startups or local businesses, clients share unreleased product details, secret business ideas, customer figures, and personal phone numbers. Uploading that to third-party cloud AI APIs creates legal and privacy risks. With open weights running locally, not a single byte leaves the freelancer's machine.

  2. $0.00 Running Cost Makes the Side Hustle Viable:
    Closed quoting platforms charge \$20 to \$50 per month. If a freelancer is just starting out or only bids on 3 projects a month, paying \$300+/year in SaaS fees is painful. Open models like Llama 3.2 cost nothing to run. 1 quote or 1,000 quotes costs \$0.00.

  3. Total Independence from Cloud Pricing & Changes:
    Closed API providers frequently deprecate model versions, hike pricing, or impose rate limits. Open-weight models are permanent assets: they will run on this laptop today, tomorrow, or 5 years from now.

  4. 100% Offline Capability:
    Freelancers frequently work from trains, cafés, or places with spotty internet. Because Llama 3.2 runs locally through Ollama, QuoteCraft works with zero internet connection.

Try It Out

Clone the repo, run python3 app.py, and test it with your own messy client chats:

👉 GitHub Repository: VIKRAM-009/quotecraft

Thanks for reading! If you have ever lost a weekend to client scope creep, give local open-weight AI a shot. 🚀

summary:
A reseller photographs forty things a week and then writes forty listings by hand. That is the tedious part of the side hustle — not the sourcing, not the shipping, the copy. Existing tools fix it by charging per listing and shipping your inventory to somebody else's cloud. I wanted to see how far a local open-weight model could get instead.

So I built Listing Studio: describe an item once and it writes a platform-shaped title, description, tags and price range for Etsy, eBay, Depop or Vinted — running entirely on your own machine.

🔗 Code: https://github.com/sank8-2/listing-studio (MIT)

Who would actually pay for this

The buyer is a one-person reseller: someone clearing a house, selling vintage finds, or running a small craft business. Their economics are small margins and large volume, and their two real costs with cloud listing tools are:

  • Per-listing pricing. When you list 200 items a month, a subscription or credit pack is a real line item. A local model costs electricity.
  • Handing over commercially sensitive data. Your stock list, your supplier names and your margins are the business. Uploading them to generate ad copy is a strange trade.

Neither of those is a technical argument. They are the reason a local tool exists at all.

How it works 

flowchart LR
  A[item notes] --> B[Python: build prompt
+ platform rules]
  B --> C[Ollama
open-weight model]
  C --> D[extract JSON]
  D --> E[Python: clamp title,
normalise tags, price band]
  E --> F[(SQLite history)]
  E --> G[listing + CSV export]

The pipeline has one deliberate rule: the model writes prose, Python decides every hard limit.

  • Etsy: 140-character title, 13 tags × 20 chars
  • eBay: 80-character title, no tags
  • Depop/Vinted: shorter titles, 5 tags

The model is never asked to count characters, because small models cannot count. finalise() clamps titles at a word boundary, lowercases and de-duplicates tags, caps their length, and reorders the price band if the model gets it backwards.

It is stdlib Python and one HTML file. No pip install, no build step, no account:

ollama pull llama3.2:1b
python3 app.py        # → http://localhost:8004

What it actually produced

Input:

item: vintage wooden birdhouse · category: garden decor · materials: pine wood · condition: good, some weathering · details: roof lifts off for cleaning; hanging hook on the back; 28 cm tall

First run, ~49 seconds on CPU, unedited:

Title: Vintage Weathered Pine Wood Birdhouse by Local Carpenter (56/140 chars)
Tags (12 returned, 13 allowed): garden decor · birdhouse · weathered pine wood · wooden birdhouse · hanging hook · pine wood birdhouse · local carpenter · handmade garden deco · garden accessory · wooden bird house · bird house for birds · decorative wooden (clipped to Etsy's 20-char tag limit mid-phrase — you can see the limit doing its work)
Price: GBP 25–40
Description: the model returned this one empty — so the deterministic fallback composer wrote it instead. That safety net is not a nice-to-have; it is the difference between an empty listing and a sellable one.

Then a second run on the identical input produced a shorter title (24 chars), only 8 tags, and a GBP 5–10 band — that is the screenshot above, and it is the honest headline: a 1B model is a drafting assistant, not an appraiser. Two runs, a 4× spread on price. The seller still sets the price. What the tool removes is the blank page, and it does that at zero marginal cost.

The part that did not work

I wanted the photo to be the input — point the camera at the item, get the listing. It is wired up, and it is not the default, for reasons worth sharing:

  • On this machine (Ollama 0.18.2, CPU-only) gemma3:1b and qwen2.5:1.5b both produced degenerate output — literal token loops like 1 1 1 1 1 even at temperature 0. Re-pulling did not help. llama3.2:1b worked fine, so the runtime is healthy and those blobs are not.
  • moondream:latest described a portrait correctly but returned symbol salad on real product photos, at 130–229 seconds per image.
  • With ~4 GB RAM free, holding a vision model and a text model at once made the model server return HTTP 500.

So I shipped text-first and left the photo field in place behind VISION_MODEL. The honest version of this project is less magical than the pitch, and it still saves the seller real time. I would rather write that down than show a screenshot of a vision pipeline I never got working reliably.

Why open matters here specifically

  • The privacy claim is structural, not a policy. There is no API key and no third-party endpoint; the app talks to 127.0.0.1:11434. You can verify it by pulling the network cable out and watching it keep working.
  • Model choice stays yours. WRITER_MODEL=llama3.1:8b is the entire upgrade path from "usable draft" to "genuinely good copy". No plan tier, no vendor deciding what you are allowed to run this month.
  • The price cannot be changed out from under you. A tool whose running cost is your own electricity does not get a pricing-page redesign that triples your bill.

For a business tool aimed at people with thin margins, those are not nice-to-haves. They are the product.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/sank8-2/listing-studio
cd listing-studio && ollama pull llama3.2:1b && python3 app.py

If you sell things on the side: I would genuinely like to know whether the output survives contact with a real listing, and where the copy falls apart. That feedback is more useful to me than a star.

  • AI-friendly workflows: Designed to complement coding agents like Claude Code and Codex.

Modern IDEs offer powerful features, but they can also consume significant system resources.

With AI coding agents becoming part of everyday development workflows, there's growing interest in development environments that prioritize speed, simplicity, and efficient resource usage.

Lithe is an interesting project to watch, although it's still worth evaluating how it compares with mature IDEs in real-world development.

title: Ledger Lift: turning a shop's handwritten sales ledger into a CSV, fully offline
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

Ledger Lift is a desktop app that reads a photo of a handwritten daily sales ledger and gives you back editable rows and a CSV.

A lot of small shops still write every sale in a paper book. To get those pages into a spreadsheet, someone has to retype them. The tools that do it automatically want you to upload your shop's records to their server and pay per page.

In Ledger Lift you pick a photo of a ledger page and press Read this page. Rows (date, item, quantity, amount) show up one at a time as the model reads them. You fix whatever it got wrong, add more pages if there are any, tick each row as reviewed, and download one CSV for all of them. The photo stays on your computer the whole time.

The people I think would pay for this are shop owners, and the bookkeepers or accountants they hand their ledgers to, who currently spend hours retyping. Since there's no server cost per page, a one-time licence makes sense.

Demo

Windows installer: Ledger Lift v0.2.1

Code

wkkny / ledger-lift

Photos of paper ledgers to spreadsheets, with a local open-weight vision model

Ledger Lift

A desktop app that turns a photo of a handwritten daily sales ledger into editable rows and a CSV. An open-weight vision model reads the page on the shop owner's own computer. Review and correct every row before using it.

The photo is sent only to the local Ollama service on the same computer. Ledger Lift does not store photos or send them to a hosted API. This is an early prototype: handwriting recognition can be wrong, so check each entry against the original page before downloading.

For the owner

  1. Open Ledger Lift. If Ollama isn't installed, the app says so, and its Download Ollama button opens the Ollama download page. Run its installer (no administrator password needed); the app notices when it finishes and carries on by itself.
  2. Ledger Lift starts Ollama for you and offers a one-time download of the reading model (about 2 GB).
  3. …
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The model is qwen3-vl:2b-instruct, an open-weight vision model, running locally through Ollama. I skipped the plain qwen3-vl:2b tag because it thinks for 30 to 100 seconds before it answers anything. If you'd rather use a different model, there's a Model picker.

The app is Electron with a React UI (shadcn/ui and Tailwind v4). The main process looks after Ollama: it starts and stops it, downloads the model (about 2 GB, once) with a progress bar, keeps it loaded between pages, and sends each row to the UI as soon as it's read. The page itself is sandboxed and has no Node access.

Most shop owners won't have Ollama installed. If it's missing, the app tells them and opens the download page, then picks up where it left off once the install is done. No admin password needed.

Getting a 2B model to do this reliably took a few tricks:

  • Photos are shrunk to 1600 px on the long edge. Full-size phone photos overflowed the model's context window.
  • The prompt tells the model to read the total for each sale from the last money column, and to copy the date from the row above when there's a ditto mark.
  • Small models sometimes get stuck writing the same rows over and over. The app spots the loop, stops, and keeps the rows from before it.

I didn't want anyone to trust the output blindly. If the model couldn't read a field or wasn't sure about a digit, that field is highlighted, and the CSV download stays off until every row is marked reviewed.

To check how accurate it is, I wrote pnpm score. It runs the real model on real pages, compares the result with answer files I typed by hand, and reports per-field accuracy, missed and invented rows, and whether the fields it got wrong were the ones it highlighted.

A GitHub Actions workflow builds and smoke-tests a Windows installer that installs for the current user only. Unit tests run against a fake Ollama server, and Playwright drives the real app end to end.

On an Apple M4, a 15-row page takes about 21 seconds, and the first row shows up after about 10.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A shop's sales ledger is private business data. With an open-weight model running locally, the pages stay on the owner's computer instead of going to a server they don't control. Once the model is downloaded, it works without internet too.

It's also why the business side works at all. There's no hosted inference bill per page, so the owner isn't tied to someone else's per-page pricing or subscription. And because the model and prompt are open, they can switch to another compatible model and see exactly how the extraction works.

It isn't perfect. Handwriting recognition gets things wrong, so every row needs checking against the page. I've scored two handwritten pages so far (about 9 and 16 rows). Amounts and quantities were mostly right, but dates and multi-word item names were weaker.

title: Roolin: rehearse the unexpected before opening night
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

What I Built

It is 19:03 on the night of the school showcase. The soloist is not in the wings. The host is looking at you, the audience is looking at the curtain, and you have about a minute to say something to the crew that does not make it worse.

Roolin is a local 3D rehearsal room for that minute.

It gives teachers, stage managers and community-theatre organisers somewhere to practise responding when a microphone fails or a performer is late. A theatre volunteer should not need to understand AI or programming to practise a difficult moment. Once the local setup is complete, the app guides them through the running order, their response and the next thing to check.

Bring your running order, review the cues proposed by Gemma, and explore a representative theatre—from the audience to backstage. At a cue, choose a disruption and write what you would actually tell the team. Gemma responds to your words with coaching and a concrete next check.

For example, when the soloist is late, you can practise briefing the crew and holding the show. Accepting that hold moves the current and later cues by five minutes while preserving the original schedule. Using a reported tested spare microphone leaves the times unchanged.

Preparation helps you work backwards from the first cue to decide when setup should begin.

The potential paid direction is team plans for drama departments and small production companies: shared running orders, collaborative rehearsals and crew-ready handoffs. Those are future possibilities. I’ve spoken with different people about whether this is something they would pay for; those conversations are exploratory, rather than confirmed purchases.

Demo

Watch the Roolin demo on YouTube

“The Show Before the Show” follows a fictional theatre volunteer facing a late soloist. Product scenes show the real Roolin app running with local Gemma and demonstrate how the rehearsal flow works.

Code

Roolin on GitHub

The application is MIT-licensed and runs locally. The README covers installation, model setup and limitations.

How I Built It

I built the theatre with Three.js, alongside a JavaScript interface and a local Node server.

Gemma 4 E4B, running through Ollama, handles two jobs: turning plain-text show notes into proposed cues with source quotations, and coaching written responses to disruptions.

Application code checks cue times, quoted text and valid schedule changes. The organiser reviews the results and approves changes.

All 18 automated tests pass, and separate browser walkthroughs exercised real local inference. AI tools assisted development and demo production.

This is a single-user prototype with two simulated disruptions. It does not detect equipment failures or certify readiness. Session data disappears on refresh; export it first.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A lot of useful technology comes with another payment or subscription. Sometimes, you can build what you need yourself using open tools and a computer you already have at home.

That is what I wanted to explore with Roolin. With suitable hardware, open weights and local inference make it possible to create a rehearsal tool without paying a cloud provider for every practice session. Hardware, electricity and initial setup still have a cost.

The person using it does not have to be the person who built it. A theatre volunteer can focus on what they would say to the crew and how to respond to a disruption, while the app provides a place to practise and review the consequences. Making those tools available to people who are not tech savvy is part of the value I want to test.

Local inference also lets rehearsal notes stay on the organiser’s computer. The application code, prompts and validation rules are available for others to inspect and adapt to their own productions.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: local Gemma powers source-linked cue drafting and response coaching—the two language tasks at the heart of Roolin.

In Nigeria, a POS operator runs a small stand with a card terminal (POS means point of sale). Many people get cash this way instead of from an ATM: the customer sends her money by bank transfer from their phone, and she hands over the same amount in cash, for a small charge. Mama POS works a stand in Port Harcourt, a city in southern Nigeria. She charges ₦150 for each ₦5,000 (₦ is the naira, Nigeria's money; that is a 3% fee). She does 10 to 20 of these a day.

Her bank, Moniepoint, sends her an email for each payment that comes in. Nigerians call this a credit alert. It is how she sees that a customer's money arrived. On 15 Oct I found her at her stand with her POS machines and asked how she keeps track. She said:

  • She writes each payment in a notebook, and it "takes long".
  • When the money does not balance, it is "a pain", so she stopped checking.
  • A customer saying "I sent it" when the money has not arrived "usually happens".
  • She pays for no tool now. When I asked if she would pay ₦5,000 a month for one that does this, she said yes.

So I built a day-book, a daily record of money in, like her notebook but filled in for her. She pastes the alert emails, and she gets:

  • Rows with the time, the amount, the kind of money and the customer's name. She types nothing. The kind is one of: a customer's transfer, phone credit she bought for herself (Nigerians call it airtime), a bank reward, or a failed transfer coming back.
  • Did it land? She types the amount a customer says they sent. The app answers "Landed", "Not seen yet", or "2 payments of this amount" and asks for the name.
  • End of day: money in, estimated charges, rows to check (reversals, the same amount twice within 10 minutes), and a text to paste into WhatsApp for the owner of the business she reports to.

All data stays in the browser. Nothing goes to a server.

App: https://mama-pos-daybook.pages.dev (the model needs a device with a working GPU, for example a laptop or a Pixel 8a; the rest works on any phone)

The video uses her 5 real alerts with the customer names redacted to "NAME". It was recorded on the live app at real speed.

Her customers' names and her balances never leave the device. These alerts show who paid her, how much, and what is in her account. A cloud API would mean sending all of that to a company she has never heard of. With an open model running in the browser, nothing is sent.

And I could see why it failed. With open weights I could test the exact model in its two versions (q4 on the GPU, int8 on the CPU), measure both, and choose. That is how I found that the CPU version cannot do this job, before it reached her.

My First User

Mama POS is the person this is for, and the name is the one she chose for this post.

What she did:

  • She told me the problem, in the words quoted above.
  • She gave me 5 of her real alert emails. I redacted the names, account numbers and references before I used them.
  • She labelled them: for each alert she told me what the money was (customer cash, her own airtime, cashback) and confirmed that the name after "TRANSFER TO" is the customer's. Those labels are the real-alert scores above.

She paid ₦5,000 up front, for the promise of it. She has not used it herself yet. Her phone cannot run Gemma (no working GPU), so for now the day-book part works on her phone and the names need a laptop. She promised to upgrade her phone. On a phone with a working GPU, like my Pixel 8a, the whole app runs on the phone.

What it does not do yet: Nomba alerts. Nomba is a second POS provider she uses, and the app reads only Moniepoint alerts.

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 3 1B runs in the browser on the user's own GPU and does the one job in the app that code could not do: reading the customer's name from free text written differently by every bank.

title: I Built NextProof Because Resume Match Scores Weren't Enough.
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

Let's be honest. Job descriptions can feel like someone combined five different roles into one and called it an entry-level position. 💀

Then comes the resume-editing ritual.

You read the job description, look at your resume, rearrange a few things, add some keywords, and hope the recruiter sees the connection.

But here's the thing , matching keywords isn't the same as understanding whether your experience actually demonstrates what a role needs.

And sometimes, you might already have the experience. Your resume just isn't making that obvious.

That's why I built NextProof.

NextProof is an AI-powered resume analysis tool that compares your resume with a job description and helps you understand the relationship between the two.

Instead of stopping at a generic match score, it breaks the analysis into an overall assessment, strengths, gaps, and actionable next steps.

The idea is simple: help you understand what your resume demonstrates, where evidence might be missing, and what you can work on next.

Because there's a difference between not having a skill and not showing evidence of that skill on your resume.

I wanted to build something that takes that difference seriously.

Demo

Live: https://nextproof.onrender.com/

Upload a PDF or DOCX resume, paste a job description, and run an analysis. You can then explore the assessment, strengths, gaps, and suggested next steps.

The application is deployed on Render, with server-side API routes handling the analysis and feedback flows.

Code

GitHub: NextProof repository

Tech stack: Next.js · JavaScript · Tailwind CSS · Gemma · Google Gen AI SDK · Supabase · Render

How I Built It

Here's the high-level flow:

Resume (PDF / DOCX) + Job Description
                 |
                 v
        Validate the inputs
                 |
                 v
        Extract resume text
                 |
                 v
        Send context to Gemma
                 |
                 v
       Parse and validate output
                 |
                 v
        Structured analysis
                 |
       +---------+----------+
       |         |          |
       v         v          v
  Assessment  Strengths    Gaps
                            |
                            v
                        Next steps

          Feedback --> Supabase

The frontend is built with Next.js and JavaScript. The analysis API route handles file validation, text extraction, and communication with the model.

For document processing, I used pdf-parse for PDF resumes and mammoth for DOCX files. Both formats need to be converted into usable text before the analysis can begin.

The application uses the Google Gen AI SDK to access hosted Gemma inference. The API key stays on the server instead of being exposed in the browser.

The model's response is parsed and validated before being returned to the frontend. The results interface then presents the analysis through separate sections rather than making users dig through one giant block of generated text.

I also built a feedback flow backed by Supabase, allowing users to share their thoughts on the usefulness and accuracy of the analysis.

Finally, I deployed the application as a Next.js web service on Render, so the frontend and server-side API routes can run together.

Why Gemma?

The part I wanted to explore was how an open-weight model could help turn two pieces of text—a resume and a job description—into a structured analysis that someone could actually use.

A job description contains requirements. A resume contains a candidate's description of their experience. Connecting the two requires more than looking for identical words; it requires interpreting context and producing feedback that makes sense to the user.

That's the role Gemma plays in NextProof.

The model receives the extracted resume text and the job description as context and generates the analysis that powers the results experience.

The surrounding application is responsible for everything that makes this usable as a product: accepting files, validating inputs, extracting text, handling inference failures, validating the returned structure, and presenting the results.

Gemma provides the language understanding; the engineering around it turns that capability into a usable workflow.

I'm particularly interested in open-weight models because they give developers more room to experiment with how AI is integrated into products. You're not limited to thinking about AI as a feature that sits behind a button. You can make decisions about model selection, inference, deployment, and how the rest of your system handles its output.

For NextProof, that meant treating the model as one component in a larger application rather than assuming that a successful API call was the entire product.

Why I Chose Hosted Inference Instead of Running Gemma Locally

I did consider running a model locally through Ollama.

But that introduced another setup step and a model download of around 1.5 GB before I could focus on the actual product experience.

Given the challenge timeline, I had a choice: spend more time setting up local inference, or use hosted Gemma inference and concentrate on getting the complete application working.

I chose the latter.

That let me spend my time on the parts that needed to come together for NextProof to be usable: document extraction, input validation, structured results, error handling, and the complete journey from resume upload to feedback.

There is a trade-off, though.

NextProof currently depends on a hosted inference service. Gemma isn't running entirely on the user's device, and the analysis requires an internet connection and an available inference endpoint.

It also means the application must account for provider errors, latency, and the costs or usage limits associated with hosted inference.

Local inference could offer different advantages, including more control over the inference environment and the possibility of processing text without sending it to an external model service. But it would also introduce model-download, hardware, and setup considerations.

For this version, I prioritised getting the complete product working over adding another inference mode.

That was a scope decision, not a claim that hosted inference is always better.

The Decisions Behind the Build

I deliberately left authentication out of the current version.

The main question I wanted to explore was whether AI could help developers understand the relationship between their resume and a job description. Sign-up and login flows wouldn't answer that question.

Authentication would also mean taking on more than a login screen: session management, account handling, and decisions about how user data should be associated with an account.

For this version, I chose to prioritise the complete resume-analysis journey over building those additional systems before validating the core experience.

That doesn't mean authentication would never make sense. If NextProof grows to support saved analyses, personal history, or persistent user accounts, those features would need to be designed alongside appropriate data-handling and privacy decisions.

For now, I wanted the core experience to work before expanding the product around it.

Why define input limits?

A resume analyser accepts files, extracts text, and sends that text through an inference pipeline. Without explicit boundaries, an unusually large document or job description can make requests slower, more expensive, or less reliable.

So I added limits to make the current implementation more predictable.

Input Limit
Uploaded resume 5 MB
Pasted job description 30,000 characters
Extracted resume text 40,000 characters

Each limit serves a different purpose.

The file-size limit bounds the uploaded document. The job-description limit constrains the pasted input. The extracted-text limit catches documents whose extracted content is too large for the intended processing scope.

The application also checks file types and whether useful text was extracted before sending the request for analysis.

These limits aren't magic numbers that guarantee accuracy, security, or perfect performance. They're explicit engineering guardrails that help control input size and keep the current workflow within a defined scope.

They can be revisited as I test more resumes, different document formats, and longer job descriptions.

I wanted NextProof to do more than work for one ideal example. Defining what it accepts, what it rejects, and how it handles failures is part of building the product.

Where This Could Go Next

There are a few directions I'd like to explore:

  • Better ways to connect each finding to the evidence in a resume and the relevant job requirement.
  • Evaluation against a broader set of real-world resumes and job descriptions.
  • More user feedback to understand where the analysis is helpful, inaccurate, or confusing.
  • Reconsidering authentication and saved analyses if there's a clear reason to introduce persistent user accounts.
  • Exploring local inference if it makes sense for privacy, cost, and the experience I want to provide.

I'd rather let actual usage and testing guide these decisions than add features just because they sound impressive on a roadmap.

Why Open Innovation Matters Here

For me, the value of open-weight AI isn't simply that a model can be downloaded or that its weights are available.

It's the room it creates for developers to experiment, understand the trade-offs, and build products around models they can choose to use and adapt.

In NextProof, Gemma is a central part of the analysis pipeline. It gives me a way to explore how open-weight AI can be applied to a practical problem, while the rest of the application handles the engineering required to make that capability usable.

The hosted setup also makes the current trade-off clear: I get to focus on the product workflow, but I depend on an external inference service. A local implementation could change that balance, but it would bring its own constraints.

There isn't one approach that's right for every product. What matters is understanding what the choice gives you, what it costs you, and whether it makes sense for the people you're building for.

That's what I wanted to explore with NextProof.

Can This Become a Side Hustle?

The problem NextProof addresses is connected to a real, recurring activity: applying for jobs and trying to understand how your experience fits a role.

A future version could explore a paid tier for more detailed analysis, saved reports, or additional workflows for job seekers. But those are possibilities, not validated business results.

I haven't established willingness to pay yet, and I don't want to pretend otherwise.

Before introducing pricing, I'd want to understand whether people find the analysis useful enough to return to it, which recommendations they trust, and what they would actually pay for.

For now, the live application is a starting point for testing the idea and learning from real users.

Final Thoughts

I keep coming back to one question: how do we build AI tools that help people make better decisions instead of simply giving them another score to worry about?

Job searching already involves enough uncertainty. You don't always know whether you're missing a skill, underselling your experience, or failing to make the connection obvious.

I wanted to build something that helps people examine that uncertainty more carefully.

NextProof is my attempt at that: a working product that uses Gemma to help turn resume and job-description text into a more structured, actionable analysis.

It's live, it has clear limitations, and there's still a lot I want to learn from people using it.

The part I wanted to explore was how an open-weight model could help turn two pieces of text—a resume and a job description—into a structured analysis that someone could actually use.

A job description contains requirements. A resume contains a candidate's description of their experience. Connecting the two requires more than looking for identical words; it requires interpreting context and producing feedback that makes sense to the user.

That's the role Gemma plays in NextProof.

The model receives the extracted resume text and the job description as context and generates the analysis that powers the results experience.

The surrounding application is responsible for everything that makes this usable as a product: accepting files, validating inputs, extracting text, handling inference failures, validating the returned structure, and presenting the results.

Gemma provides the language understanding; the engineering around it turns that capability into a usable workflow.

I'm particularly interested in open-weight models because they give developers more room to experiment with how AI is integrated into products. You're not limited to thinking about AI as a feature that sits behind a button. You can make decisions about model selection, inference, deployment, and how the rest of your system handles its output.

For NextProof, that meant treating the model as one component in a larger application rather than assuming that a successful API call was the entire product.

Why I Chose Hosted Inference Instead of Running Gemma Locally

I did consider running a model locally through Ollama.

But that introduced another setup step and a model download of around 1.5 GB before I could focus on the actual product experience.

Given the challenge timeline, I had a choice: spend more time setting up local inference, or use hosted Gemma inference and concentrate on getting the complete application working.

I chose the latter.

That let me spend my time on the parts that needed to come together for NextProof to be usable: document extraction, input validation, structured results, error handling, and the complete journey from resume upload to feedback.

There is a trade-off, though.

NextProof currently depends on a hosted inference service. Gemma isn't running entirely on the user's device, and the analysis requires an internet connection and an available inference endpoint.

It also means the application must account for provider errors, latency, and the costs or usage limits associated with hosted inference.

Local inference could offer different advantages, including more control over the inference environment and the possibility of processing text without sending it to an external model service. But it would also introduce model-download, hardware, and setup considerations.

For this version, I prioritised getting the complete product working over adding another inference mode.

That was a scope decision, not a claim that hosted inference is always better.

The Decisions Behind the Build

I deliberately left authentication out of the current version.

The main question I wanted to explore was whether AI could help developers understand the relationship between their resume and a job description. Sign-up and login flows wouldn't answer that question.

Authentication would also mean taking on more than a login screen: session management, account handling, and decisions about how user data should be associated with an account.

For this version, I chose to prioritise the complete resume-analysis journey over building those additional systems before validating the core experience.

That doesn't mean authentication would never make sense. If NextProof grows to support saved analyses, personal history, or persistent user accounts, those features would need to be designed alongside appropriate data-handling and privacy decisions.

For now, I wanted the core experience to work before expanding the product around it.

Why define input limits?

A resume analyser accepts files, extracts text, and sends that text through an inference pipeline. Without explicit boundaries, an unusually large document or job description can make requests slower, more expensive, or less reliable.

So I added limits to make the current implementation more predictable.

Input Limit
Uploaded resume 5 MB
Pasted job description 30,000 characters
Extracted resume text 40,000 characters

Each limit serves a different purpose.

The file-size limit bounds the uploaded document. The job-description limit constrains the pasted input. The extracted-text limit catches documents whose extracted content is too large for the intended processing scope.

The application also checks file types and whether useful text was extracted before sending the request for analysis.

These limits aren't magic numbers that guarantee accuracy, security, or perfect performance. They're explicit engineering guardrails that help control input size and keep the current workflow within a defined scope.

They can be revisited as I test more resumes, different document formats, and longer job descriptions.

I wanted NextProof to do more than work for one ideal example. Defining what it accepts, what it rejects, and how it handles failures is part of building the product.

Where This Could Go Next

There are a few directions I'd like to explore:

  • Better ways to connect each finding to the evidence in a resume and the relevant job requirement.
  • Evaluation against a broader set of real-world resumes and job descriptions.
  • More user feedback to understand where the analysis is helpful, inaccurate, or confusing.
  • Reconsidering authentication and saved analyses if there's a clear reason to introduce persistent user accounts.
  • Exploring local inference if it makes sense for privacy, cost, and the experience I want to provide.

I'd rather let actual usage and testing guide these decisions than add features just because they sound impressive on a roadmap.

Why Open Innovation Matters Here

For me, the value of open-weight AI isn't simply that a model can be downloaded or that its weights are available.

It's the room it creates for developers to experiment, understand the trade-offs, and build products around models they can choose to use and adapt.

In NextProof, Gemma is a central part of the analysis pipeline. It gives me a way to explore how open-weight AI can be applied to a practical problem, while the rest of the application handles the engineering required to make that capability usable.

The hosted setup also makes the current trade-off clear: I get to focus on the product workflow, but I depend on an external inference service. A local implementation could change that balance, but it would bring its own constraints.

There isn't one approach that's right for every product. What matters is understanding what the choice gives you, what it costs you, and whether it makes sense for the people you're building for.

That's what I wanted to explore with NextProof.

Can This Become a Side Hustle?

The problem NextProof addresses is connected to a real, recurring activity: applying for jobs and trying to understand how your experience fits a role.

A future version could explore a paid tier for more detailed analysis, saved reports, or additional workflows for job seekers. But those are possibilities, not validated business results.

I haven't established willingness to pay yet, and I don't want to pretend otherwise.

Before introducing pricing, I'd want to understand whether people find the analysis useful enough to return to it, which recommendations they trust, and what they would actually pay for.

For now, the live application is a starting point for testing the idea and learning from real users.

Final Thoughts

I keep coming back to one question: how do we build AI tools that help people make better decisions instead of simply giving them another score to worry about?

Job searching already involves enough uncertainty. You don't always know whether you're missing a skill, underselling your experience, or failing to make the connection obvious.

I wanted to build something that helps people examine that uncertainty more carefully.

NextProof is my attempt at that: a working product that uses Gemma to help turn resume and job-description text into a more structured, actionable analysis.

It's live, it has clear limitations, and there's still a lot I want to learn from people using it.

title: "Behind Lulu" is not an address: a $2 fine-tune that reads addresses like a dispatcher
summary:
What I Built

Lulu is a hypermarket chain you find all over the Gulf. "Behind Lulu, call before coming" is what a customer in Dubai types when they mean "I'll explain on the phone". A courier who sends that parcel out without calling pays for the failed trip.

India has its own version: "near Hanuman mandir, Bandra West", often with no house number. A driver gets 120 of these on a morning route, and many are cash on delivery, so a failed stop means the parcel comes back and the seller never gets paid.

Pata ("address" in Hindi and Urdu) reads each address before the van leaves and answers DELIVERABLE, CALL_FIRST (with a call script) or LIKELY_FAIL. It also splits the address into building, flat, street, area, landmark and PIN (India's postal code). Real outputs from the deployed model:

What the customer typed Order Pata says
Flat 1203, Marina Pinnacle Tower, Dubai Marina UAE, cash DELIVERABLE
behind Lulu Hypermarket Al Barsha, call before coming UAE, cash CALL_FIRST:"Could you confirm your building or house number? Payment is cash on delivery."
H.No 45, MG Road, Bengaluru 560001 India, order's PIN field says 110001 LIKELY_FAIL: the address says Bengaluru, 110001 is Delhi

The short version: simple rules already match the tuned model at saying deliver, call or hold. What a $2 fine-tune adds is reading the address:

Indian addresses (150 test rows) Building found Area found
My rules 47% 14%
Qwen3.5-4B, untrained 53% 76%
Pata (trained 4B) 90% 87%

A field counts as found when it exactly matches the human-tagged field in the source dataset, ignoring case and spacing.

Who I expect would pay: couriers and cash-on-delivery sellers in India and the Gulf, where "behind Lulu" is in no postal database. Pata costs about $0.15 to $0.17 per 1,000 parcels to run, and two training runs cost $5.35 in total.

Demo

Try it: https://pata-gw9g.onrender.com

It runs on Render's free tier, so the first request after a quiet spell can take up to a minute. Try "behind Lulu Hypermarket Al Barsha" with cash on delivery, then add a flat and building number. The repo has a Deploy to Render button for your own copy.

Code

AbdulWasih05 / pata

Dispatch triage for couriers: a fine-tuned 4B model decides DELIVERABLE, CALL_FIRST or LIKELY_FAIL before the van leaves.

Pata

Dispatch triage for couriers. Pata reads a raw customer address plus order context and returns a decision before the van leaves: DELIVERABLE, CALL_FIRST, or LIKELY_FAIL, with normalised fields, a one-line driver note, and the reason.

Entry for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2: Side Hustle. Built by Abdul Wasih (@iamwasih).

Live demo: https://pata-24o3.onrender.com (free instance; the first request after a quiet spell can take up to a minute). Serving checkpoint: run 2 (see train/RUNS.md, eval/results.md).

How it works

        |
        v
 FastAPI gateway (Render)  ---- Sentry agent trace per request
   1. rules_prelabel   pata/rules.py, always computed
   2. chat             tuned Qwen3.5-4B, Tinker OpenAI-compatible endpoint
                       (hedged: a 2nd request after 1.5 s, first answer wins)
   3. schema.validate  pata/schema.py (pydantic)
   4. rules_fallback   only if the model call fails or its JSON is invalid
        |
        v
 decision + normalised fields + driver note
…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

1. Rules first

Before any AI, I wrote down how a careful dispatcher decides, as plain Python functions with tests (pata/rules.py). For example, an Indian address with no PIN code gets CALL_FIRST, because a courier cannot route it. Every judgement call like that is written up in DECISIONS.md. The rules did two jobs: they labelled the training data, and they are the backup answer if the model ever fails.

2. Data

  • India: real company-registry addresses from public Hugging Face datasets (indian-addresses-gold, indian-address-parsing-synthetic, Apache 2.0), roughed up with landmarks, typos, missing PINs and Hinglish like "mandir ke paas" ("near the temple").
  • UAE: synthetic, because no public Gulf address dataset exists. A generator writes Makani numbers (Dubai's building ID), PO boxes, Arabic script and "will share location on WhatsApp".

About 6,000 training examples, and no real customer addresses.

3. Fine-tuning on Tinker

Tinker is Thinking Machines' fine-tuning service: you write the training loop in Python and it runs on their GPUs. I took Qwen3.5-4B, a small open model (Apache 2.0), and trained a LoRA adapter on it. LoRA trains a small add-on to the model instead of retraining all of it, so a run took 13 to 19 minutes and cost $2 to $3 (train/RUNS.md). A FastAPI app on Render serves it, checks every reply against a strict schema, and falls back to the rules if anything is off.

4. The run that went wrong

My first run looked worse than expected on India: on 45 parcels where my rules said hold or call, the model said DELIVERABLE. I read all 45. In 30 of them, the model was right and my rules were wrong. "H.No 323, Balaji Heights" was marked "missing flat number", but the house number is the flat.

I fixed the rule, added tests, relabelled the data and trained a second run, which serves today. The lesson: a model trained on your rules can still check those rules, but only if you read the cases where the two disagree.

Sentry: the mystery 6-second requests

Every request is traced in Sentry's AI agent monitoring: the rules check, the model call with its token counts, and the schema check each show up as a span. Traces store lengths and decisions, not the address text.

The traces showed something logs would have hidden. Model calls took either about 1 second or about 6 seconds, with almost nothing in between, and with the same token counts. So the model was not writing more; something upstream was holding some requests for five seconds.

The fix is an old trick, a hedged request: if the first call has not answered in 1.5 seconds, send it again and use whichever answer arrives first. Each span records whether it was hedged.

40 requests each way (benchmark, results):

Before After hedging
Typical (p50) 1.15 s 1.04 s
Slow end (p90) 6.19 s 2.92 s
Requests over 5 s 10 of 40 0 of 40

Six of the forty sent a second call, so hedging adds at most 15% to the cost.

Eval

Testing against my rules would only show that the model copied them. So a separate AI reviewer (Claude) labelled 150 test addresses per market, seeing my written definitions but never the rules' answers or code. Of those, 106 India and 77 UAE parcels should be called or held; the rest (44 and 73) are fine to deliver.

System Correct (India / UAE) India wrongly approved Good parcels held (India / UAE) Cost per 1,000 (India / UAE)
Qwen3.5-4B, untrained 43% / 25% 28 of 106 4 of 44 / 56 of 73 $0.33 / $0.31
Qwen3.5-397B, untrained 49% / 57% 7 of 106 22 of 44 / 33 of 73 $2.20 / $2.01
My rules alone 87% / 85% 9 of 106 3 of 44 / 23 of 73 $0
Pata (trained 4B) 86% / 85% 11 of 106 4 of 44 / 22 of 73 $0.17 / $0.15

Both untrained models got the same instructions plus a JSON format description, with thinking off. That longer prompt, and their longer answers, is why they cost more. On UAE, wrongly approved was 0 of 77 for everyone but the 397B (1 of 77). Full tables: eval/results.md.

What it means: training doubled the 4B's accuracy on India and tripled it on UAE, and it beats a model 100 times its size at a thirteenth of the cost. That bigger model only looks safe because it holds half the good parcels. On the three-way decision, though, the trained model ties my rules, agreeing with them on all but 9 of 300 addresses. Its real win is reading the building and area, as in the table at the top.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Local quirks are teachable. You cannot fine-tune a closed API on "Al Nahda without an emirate". One $2 run on an open model took UAE from 25% to 85%.
  • Addresses stay in-house. The weights are open, so a courier can run them on its own machine instead of sending names, phones and cash orders to a third party.
  • Nothing is locked away. Rules, data generator, training and eval are all in the repo.

Honest limitations

  • The test labels come from an AI reviewer, not real delivery outcomes.
  • The test set is 150 addresses per market.
  • The UAE data is synthetic, generated from real patterns.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Tinker: two LoRA runs of Qwen3.5-4B, evaluated against the base model, a 397B model and the rules, including the failed run. The live demo serves from the Tinker checkpoint.
  • Best Use of Render: the app runs from a one-click render.yaml blueprint.
  • Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing: traces exposed the 6-second requests, and the hedging fix removed them.

Built by @iamwasih.

title: Day 17 of Building Crowdwide — Trying to Bring Users Back!!
summary:
I was building Crowdwide, a social media platform I started working on on 9 Sept 2026 (the day I created the GitHub repo).

That was the day when it was at 0, and now, after 1 month and 10 days, it has lots of features and 11 users!!

But I noticed that users are there, but they barely come back.

So I decided to focus on getting users now.

so what new did i change to achieve this in crowdwide?

there was no common social media feature left to implement at this point!!

so now i just thought that i should call the users back by notifications.

i implemented these:

After 24 hours away: a community question they can answer. It picks an open question that matches their interests and has few replies. If none exists, it sends Today's Question.

After 3 days: the most active discussion matching their interests, plus a line on what's new this week (new posts, members, communities).

After 7 days: a last "what you missed" note with replies, likes, and new followers on their posts, plus top posts. It says it's the last reminder.

Channels: each goes by email, by push if they have push notifications turned on, and as a notification waiting in the app. If there's nothing worth saying, nothing is sent.

and these were for when the user isn't coming back, but if the user comes back, what will he do??

like no task??

so i came up with that... that i should give him some task, like answering any question. not a maths or physics question lol.

i mean a funny, short, concise question.

and u will be able to answer other people's questions too!!

also, the Privacy page now mentions the reminders.

thinking of adding more things now... maybe today you'll see something like streaks and badges... that's under development right now!!

reddit...

also, to get ideas for getting more users, i was checking out other similar platforms that match Crowdwide's category.

like reddit!!

and idk why this happens only to me.

i was on reddit, opened a page on r/startupideaindia, and saw a post from a user saying that he was a tea seller who wanted to get more buyers but wasn't very professional.

he wanted a B2B setup, but he didn't have enough funding and was self-funded, so he was asking for advice and tips.

i commented below with something like:

create hype or try something unique.

like, with tea, provide unique-looking cups or teabags that look normal but show a beautiful picture when dipped in tea.

also, if you're targeting indian people, give them something special on festivals.

like diwali special cups.

india is a price-sensitive market. make them feel like they paid less and got more!!

and they just removed my content, ngl. it was written by me 1000%.

WHYYYY???

so i decided to never implement any useless algorithm on Crowdwide like reddit, which does this.

and while posting the comment, they said i had to wait 3 minutes. i waited 3 mins, then posted it and...

they just removed it for no reason!!

but i also wanted to know how these bots work.

should i implement something like this on Crowdwide??

but fine!!

i don't need bots on Crowdwide.

less users but real users!!

Links:

🌐 Live website: https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

💻 GitHub repository: https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide

title: Discuss the trade-offs before anyone writes code
summary:
Most multi-agent setups add more roles before they add a shared brief.

What usually helps: connect several models to one project, let them argue the trade-offs, keep verification separate from the draft, and require an explicit human OK before the main branch moves.

That is the workflow Brainstorm is built around — a shell for discussion → task split → independent checks → your publish gate. Model usage stays on your own eligible accounts (BYOK); the license does not sell model credits.

Linux has a released build. Windows remains a preview.
